cls: Trace element / mineral supplement - essential micronutrient (zinc salt)
quick: Deficiency: ~220 mg zinc sulfate (50 mg elemental) once or more daily
Best on empty stomach; take with food if GI upset occurs
Safe at recommended intakes; used when indicated
No adjustment orally; adjust parenteral zinc in renal disease
Adjust parenteral dosing in significant hepatic/biliary loss
summary: Zinc sulfate is a zinc salt used to prevent and treat zinc deficiency and as a zinc source in parenteral nutrition. Zinc is an essential trace element required for the function of numerous enzymes, immune function, wound healing, growth and development. Oral zinc sulfate is also used adjunctively for acute childhood diarrhea per WHO/UNICEF guidance. Gastrointestinal upset is the main adverse effect; chronic high-dose use can induce copper deficiency, and zinc impairs absorption of several antibiotics.
indications: Treatment and prevention of zinc deficiency
Adjunctive treatment of acute diarrhea in children (WHO/UNICEF)
Increased requirements (malabsorption, burns, prolonged diarrhea, acrodermatitis enteropathica)

dosage.d: 220 mg zinc sulfate (approximately 50 mg elemental zinc)
dosage.n: Titrate to severity and serum levels
For 10-14 days (10 mg/day if under 6 months)

dosage.d: 2.5-4 mg elemental zinc/day IV (more if losses)
dosage.n: Increase with GI losses; adjust per monitoring
Lifelong; titrate to clinical response and levels

admin: Take on an empty stomach, 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals, for best absorption
If gastric irritation occurs, take with food (accepting reduced absorption)
Separate from iron, calcium, antibiotics (tetracyclines/quinolones) and bisphosphonates by several hours
For childhood diarrhea, continue the full course even after stools improve and continue ORS and feeding
moa: Zinc is an essential cofactor for over 300 metalloenzymes and numerous transcription factors (zinc fingers), participating in protein and nucleic acid synthesis, cell division, immune function, wound healing, taste/smell and antioxidant defense (as part of copper-zinc superoxide dismutase). Supplementation corrects deficiency and restores these zinc-dependent processes; in diarrhea it improves intestinal mucosal integrity and immune response.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to zinc salts or product components
relative: Conditions where reduced copper would be harmful (with chronic high-dose use)
monitor: Serum zinc and copper with prolonged/high-dose therapy
Alkaline phosphatase (zinc-dependent) as a marker of status

preg: Zinc is safe and required during pregnancy at recommended intakes and may be supplemented when deficiency or increased need exists. Avoid chronic high-dose supplementation beyond requirements.
lact: Compatible with breastfeeding at recommended intakes; zinc is a normal constituent of breast milk and supplementation to meet requirements is acceptable.
renal: Oral supplementation needs no specific adjustment. In parenteral nutrition, zinc dosing may need adjustment in renal impairment based on serum levels.
hepatic: No oral dose adjustment is generally needed. In hepatic/biliary disease with increased GI losses, parenteral zinc requirements may rise; adjust per monitoring.

moderate: Tetracycline and fluoroquinolone antibiotics (zinc chelation reduces antibiotic absorption - separate doses by 2-6 hours)
Penicillamine (reduced absorption of both; separate administration)
Copper (high-dose zinc lowers copper absorption - risk of copper deficiency)
minor: Iron and calcium supplements (mutual reduction in absorption)
interactions.food: Phytates (whole grains, legumes) and dairy reduce zinc absorption; take on an empty stomach when possible
interactions.alcohol: No direct interaction; chronic alcohol use can lower zinc status
interactions.diagnostics: Affects serum zinc and copper measurements; very high doses can lower serum copper and ceruloplasmin

serious: Copper deficiency (anemia, leukopenia/neutropenia) with chronic high-dose use
emergency: Severe vomiting/dehydration after large acute ingestion
Profound neutropenia from copper deficiency (chronic overuse)

monitoring: Serum copper and CBC with prolonged or high-dose therapy
Alkaline phosphatase as a functional marker of zinc status
Clinical response (wound healing, dermatitis, diarrhea resolution)
counsel: Take on an empty stomach for best absorption; if it upsets your stomach, take it with food
Separate from antibiotics, iron and calcium by a few hours
For a child's diarrhea, give the full 10-14 day course along with oral rehydration and continued feeding
Do not take high doses long term without advice - excess zinc can cause copper deficiency
Report ongoing nausea, unusual tiredness, or frequent infections
pk: Repletion of deficiency develops over days to weeks; GI effects can be immediate
Serum zinc peaks within ~2-4 hours of an oral dose
Tissue biological half-life of zinc is prolonged (days); homeostatically regulated
Body stores buffer levels; daily intake maintains status
Store at room temperature, protected from moisture
pearls: Zinc absorption is reduced by phytates and dairy - take on an empty stomach when tolerated
Chronic high-dose zinc induces copper deficiency causing anemia and neutropenia - monitor copper
Chelates tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones - separate doses to preserve antibiotic efficacy
WHO/UNICEF recommend 10-14 days of zinc for acute childhood diarrhea to reduce duration and recurrence
Different salts differ in elemental zinc content - dose by elemental zinc (zinc sulfate is ~23% elemental zinc)
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered, unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip it - do not double up. For childhood diarrhea, simply continue the daily course.
overdose: Acute zinc sulfate overdose causes nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, and diarrhea; very large doses can cause corrosive GI injury and systemic effects. Chronic excess causes copper deficiency. Management is supportive with fluids; milk or chelation may be considered for large acute ingestions, and copper is supplemented for deficiency once zinc is reduced.
